name: Lützen
summary: Wittgenstein and Blücher, hoping to catch Napoleon's army strung out on the march to Leipzig, fell on Ney's corps in its villages south of Lützen. All afternoon the Prussians and Russians fought Ney's conscripts for Gross-Görschen, Klein-Görschen, Rahna and Kaja, which changed hands again and again; Scharnhorst was mortally wounded. Napoleon brought up his other corps from both flanks, and at dusk the Young Guard retook the villages behind a great battery. The allies withdrew in good order, but Napoleon, with almost no cavalry, could not pursue.

forces.name: Souham's Division
forces.summary: Ney's leading division, camped in the four villages south of Lützen, Gross-Görschen, Klein-Görschen, Rahna and Kaja, when Blücher's Prussians came at it at midday. Its conscripts were driven from village to village and came back again and again; Souham's division lost more than a third of its strength in the day.
notes: Built from A Clash of Eagles' French 1812 list, the nearest to 1813: there is no list for the army Napoleon raised after Russia, largely of conscripts and of battalions drawn from depots all over the Empire.
After Nafziger's order of battle for Lützen, with strengths of 25 April.
Its battalions were mostly young conscripts of the classes of 1813 and 1814. They are rated as ordinary Line, as they fought: the list's Wavering or Morale 5 would suit those who broke more readily.
Most of its regiments were provisional: two depot battalions of different regiments put together, each shown as its two battalions.
Its two provisional light regiments, where the list allows one light regiment in a division, and Chasseraux's four regiments, where the list allows three in a brigade, show as historical departures.
Regimental guns were lost in Russia and not replaced, so the division has none.
The division's two foot batteries, where the list allows one, show as a historical departure.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces.

forces.summary: Ney's reserve, at Starsiedel when the battle began, it came into Kaja in the afternoon and retook the village when the Prussian Guard and Yorck's men had driven the others out.

forces.name: Marchand's Division
forces.summary: Ney's German division, Baden, Hessian and Frankfurt troops, on the left round Klein-Görschen and Eisdorf, which held its ground against the Prussian and Russian attacks there through the afternoon.
notes: Built from A Clash of Eagles' Confederation of the Rhine 1812 list, the nearest to 1813.
After Nafziger's order of battle for Lützen, with strengths of 25 April.
The 1st Hessian Light Regiment is shown as the list's Hessian Guard Fusiliers, the only Hessian light troops it has.
The list's Hessian brigade has only Guard regiments, so the 2nd Hessian (Line) Regiment and the Frankfurt battalion are a Rheinbund brigade.
The Baden battery had four guns and the Hessians half a battery of three, each shown as a half battery.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces; but Hessian Line and Frankfurt at 7, the most the list allows.

missing.name: Laboissière's and Jett's cavalry
missing.reason: The 10th Hussars, Baden Dragoons, Hessian Chevau-légers and Württemberg light horse Nafziger lists with the division were Ney's corps cavalry, and the Confederation list has no French hussars.

forces.name: Dumoustier's Young Guard
forces.summary: Napoleon's last reserve. As the light failed, with Kaja lost again and Ney's divisions spent, he sent sixteen battalions of the Young Guard in four columns under Mortier, behind a battery of seventy guns, through Kaja and Rahna; the allies gave up the villages and drew off in the night.
notes: Built from A Clash of Eagles' Imperial Guard 1812 list, the nearest to 1813.
After Nafziger's order of battle for Lützen, with strengths of 25 April.
Nafziger lists the 6th Tirailleurs in both Berthezène's and Tindal's brigades; it is shown once, with Tindal.
The 2nd Old Guard Foot Battery of 12-pdrs, attached to the division, is in the Guard artillery reserve, as the list takes it.
Three Young Guard brigades, where the list allows two without Old Guard, and Tindal's battery in a brigade of four battalions, where the list wants six, show as historical departures.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces.

forces.name: Berg's Corps
forces.summary: Wittgenstein's Russian infantry in Yorck's second line, which came up behind the Prussians in the afternoon and fought for Kaja and Rahna beside them; its battalions had fought the whole of 1812 under Wittgenstein on the Dvina.
notes: Built from A Clash of Eagles' Russian list, which covers 1812-15.
After Nafziger's order of battle for Lützen, with strengths of 25 April.
By the spring of 1813 Russian infantry regiments were down to a single field battalion each, the rest having gone back to recruit; each regiment is shown as its one battalion.
The Grand Duchess Catherine's Battalion, raised on her estates in 1812, is shown as Volunteer Jäger attached to the Sevsk regiment.
The position battery, with fewer battalions than the list wants for it, shows as a historical departure.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces; but 2 of the 4 brigade commanders at 7, as the list rates at most half of them higher.

forces.name: Eugen of Württemberg's Corps
forces.summary: On the allied left, it came up late in the morning and pushed towards Starsiedel against Marmont's corps, then was drawn into the fighting round Kaja; at nightfall it covered the allied withdrawal.
notes: Built from A Clash of Eagles' Russian list, which covers 1812-15.
After Nafziger's order of battle for Lützen, with strengths of 25 April.
By the spring of 1813 Russian infantry regiments were down to a single field battalion each, the rest having gone back to recruit; each regiment is shown as its one battalion.
Prince Eugen of Württemberg is the book's named commander. His corps was Shakhovskoy's 3rd and St Priest's 4th Divisions, shown together.
The Ukrainian Cossack regiments, raised in 1812, are shown as Mounted Cossacks.
Two Jäger brigades, three-regiment infantry brigades and three light batteries, more than the list allows for the corps' ten line battalions, show as historical departures.

Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces, except the book's named Major General Eugene von Württemberg, with his own rating; but 3 of the 5 brigade commanders at 7, as the list rates at most half of them higher.

forces.name: Blücher's Corps
forces.formation: Zieten's, Klüx's and Röder's brigades, with Dolffs's cavalry
forces.summary: The Silesian brigades of Zieten and Klüx, which opened the attack on Gross-Görschen and fought for the villages all afternoon; Röder's Brandenburg brigade with the Guard infantry, which stormed Klein-Görschen and Kaja; and Dolffs's Garde du Corps and cuirassiers, which charged the French squares at dusk, Dolffs killed.
notes: Built from Albion Triumphant's Prussian 1815 list, the nearest to 1813: its Prussian Infantry Brigade is the 1813 brigade, the size of another army's division, with line, reserve and Landwehr battalions.
After Nafziger's order of battle for Lützen, from Plotho.
Blücher is the book's named commander.
A Prussian brigade was the size of another army's division, so the whole corps is here. Take the brigades you want; each is a force in itself.

In the spring of 1813 the brigades had no Landwehr yet: each was two line regiments, with grenadier, reserve and Jäger battalions besides, so most have more line regiments, or more battalions in a regiment, than the list's brigade takes, which shows as historical departures.

Battalions of different regiments that served together are grouped as a regiment, as the list takes them. Reserve battalions are the list's Musketeers; grenadier battalions are Musketeers with its Veteran upgrade.
Brigades of three regiments or more have a Subordinate Commander, named where the order of battle names the brigade's infantry commander.

The list has no Guard: the Guard Infantry Regiment and the Normal Battalion are Musketeers and Fusiliers, and the Guard Jäger and Wedell's Guard Volunteer Jäger are the list's attached Schützen, its only Jäger battalion a brigade takes; with the Silesian Schützen, three where the list allows one in the army, they show as historical departures.

The list has no cuirassiers or Guard cavalry: the Garde du Corps and the East Prussian, Silesian and Brandenburg Cuirassiers are its Dragoons, its only heavy cavalry, and the Guard Light Cavalry its Hussars. Jürgass's three cuirassier regiments, where the list's brigade takes two Dragoons, show as a historical departure.
The Silesian Schützen are the list's attached Schützen battalion.
More cavalry brigades than the list allows for the infantry, and brigades of two-squadron regiments, show as historical departures; regiments of two or three squadrons are shown at full size.

Batteries beyond the one each brigade takes are in the corps artillery, as the list's reserve takes them; more than it allows, or a reserve horse battery with fewer brigades than the list wants for it, show as historical departures.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces, except the book's named Field Marshal Prince Blücher, with his own rating.

forces.name: Yorck's Corps
forces.formation: Hünerbein's and Horn's brigades, with Steinmetz's reserve
forces.summary: The old Prussian auxiliary corps of 1812, the left of Yorck's second line beside Berg's Russians, which came up in the afternoon and fought for Kaja.
notes: Built from Albion Triumphant's Prussian 1815 list, the nearest to 1813: its Prussian Infantry Brigade is the 1813 brigade, the size of another army's division, with line, reserve and Landwehr battalions.
After Nafziger's order of battle for Lützen, from Plotho.

Battalions of different regiments that served together are grouped as a regiment, as the list takes them. Reserve battalions are the list's Musketeers; grenadier battalions are Musketeers with its Veteran upgrade.

The Leib Regiment's fusilier battalion, a regiment of its own in Hünerbein's brigade, and Steinmetz's reserve of the one Colberg Regiment, where the list's brigade wants two, show as historical departures.

The Lithuanian Dragoons from Hünerbein and the 2nd Combined Dragoons (two squadrons each of the 1st West Prussian and Brandenburg Dragoons) from Horn are together as the corps cavalry, with Steinmetz's horse battery; the 2nd Leib Hussars are Steinmetz's attached hussars.
The East Prussian Jäger were detached to Kleist.
